utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39 & 40-PT, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik and Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Judge May, Judge Kwon. My name is Mark Harmon. Appearing with me is Mr. Tieger from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Deyan Brashich with Nikola Kostich for the Krajisnik Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Robert Pavich with Eugene O'Sullivan and Peter Murphy for the Plavsic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The purpose of this hearing is a Status Conference in this case in which a number of matters have to be dealt with, chiefly to establish a timetable for the trial. Mr. Harmon, it may be that you can assist in that. A number of matters were dealt with at the meeting which I held with the parties. Perhaps you can give an update on the various matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Judge May, I'd be glad to. The first item that we discussed in the meeting last month was the issue of 92 bis statements. We are prepared today to -- tomorrow to turn over to the Defence 62 of those 92 bis statements with attestations, and I am in the process of checking with my investigators as to the remaining number. Should there be remaining 150 bis attestations that were completed on the most recent mission, it's my desire to turn those over forthwith to the Defence. The second point that we discussed at the meeting was the issue of expert reports. To summarise, the Defence was in need of a Defence expert and needed an expert appointed by OLAD to assist them in reviewing the exhumation reports, and it was agreed that within 30 days of the appointment of that expert, the Defence would get back to the Prosecution and inform the Prosecution whether they accepted the statement of the expert. It is my understanding that on the 6th of December, a request for the appointment of an expert was made to OLAD. So we await the decision by OLAD as to the appointment of that expert and then matters can progress in the manner which I have outlined. The third issue that we discussed was the issue of adjudicated facts, and at the last meeting, the parties had agreed to identify adjudicated facts for consideration under Rule 94(B) by the 31st of January, 2002, and we undertook to attempt to reach an agreement on some or all of those by the 1st of March, 2002. I can report to the Court that we have prepared today a submission of adjudicated facts that we have identified. These adjudicated facts are facts that have been identified from the various decisions that take us up to today's date. I suspect there may be some additional adjudicated facts but I'm confident that the majority of those facts that we believe have been adjudicated and we have identified we will give over to the Defence today. So we're ahead of schedule, considerably ahead of schedule, on that project. The issue of the untranslated documents, it is my understanding that -- and I will defer to my colleague Mr. Tieger in just a moment. He's been principally dealing with that issue. It's my understanding that there is a new regime, so to say, as to who controls the documents and the rate of production of translation of those documents that will soon be undertaken. Mr. Tieger can address that issue in just a moment with Your Honours. The next issue that we raised at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Shall we deal with the untranslated documents while we're still on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will be glad to defer to my colleague Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, if you would tell us what the position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour. Mr. President and Your Honour, as you will recall, we were previously operating on the basis of two translation schedules. The original one, for a period of time, envisioned approximately 1.000 pages a month. The latter schedule, which was reported in our last meeting, appeared to be 700 a month. It's my understanding, and I don't wish to pre-empt any clarification by the Registry on an issue which I understand they are grappling with seriously, that an institution-wide regime is about to be implemented which will -- which may result in changes to the individual allocations to particular cases. Essentially, that means that we cannot report a fixed number of pages per month on which to base estimations of the completion of our untranslated documents. Obviously, we will be working as closely as possible with whatever instrument is formed to allocate particular pages to particular cases, whether that's a committee or otherwise, but I think it's fair to report our present understanding that the assurance of 700 pages upon which we previously relied should no longer be taken for granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What effect is that going to have on the preparation of this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I think it's difficult to say. I don't know whether or not an institution-wide regime will result in any dramatic change in the number of pages we can expect a month. Obviously, we hope not. In addition, during meetings with the Defence, we have discussed or begun discussing possible ways to reduce the number of pages needed for translation through agreements between the parties. Just to say two things: Number one, we haven't received estimations yet which tell us with any certainty whether or not the previous projections will be reduced or increased, and if it turns out that we are receiving fewer pages per month, we would like to work as creatively and as energetically as possible to adopt procedures which will reduce our own need for -- within the case for translated pages. At the same time, unilaterally, we will continue to look at our exhibits to see if that can be culled in such a way to reduce the number of necessary translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Clearly, if it's possible one way or another to reduce this backlog, it's going to help the readiness of the case. So I for one would encourage very much agreement between the parties as to the disclosure of untranslated documents or whatever other regime can be put into place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We will certainly take those words to heart, Your Honour. And as you know, we have been successful to date in our efforts to achieve consensus between the Defence and the Prosecution. I am optimistic we can continue to do so and those efforts will certainly be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will continue then with the discussion about what occurred at the last conference and where we are in respect of each of those items. We had agreed as well to provide the Defence with untranslated documents as soon as possible, approximately 12.000, and we are prepared at this point to provide to the Defence, on a disk, 500 copies of documents. In addition, we will provide to the Defence, by the 22nd of December of this year, an additional 2.000 documents. Those documents will be in B/C/S and in English translation. That brings me to a related issue, and that is that we had undertaken to provide to the Defence a copy of all of our discovery materials on a disk, with a more powerful search engine, Zy 4, and that was at the last conference a procedure that was being tested by the technical people of this organisation. I am told that there are difficulties in terms of absorbing these materials onto a disk in a very quick fashion. I have discussed this. I've raised the issue with the Defence today. We're prepared, in the alternative, to provide hard copies of all of those pages to the Defence. So we have given the Defence a choice, and the choice is wait for those documents to be copied on a disk. I was asked when I thought the completion of the burning of those documents onto a disk would be done. I didn't have an answer for them this afternoon. I'm endeavouring to get an answer for them, but the alternative choice for the Defence is to receive hard copies, and we're able to furnish hard copies very quickly of those outstanding documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me see if I have it right. 500 copied documents today on a disk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 2.000 documents in translated form on the 22nd of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct. In B/C/S and in translated form. Which leaves us with a remainder, and that's where the problem develops. And I have explained the problem to the Defence and given them a choice, and they will get back to me as to whether they want the remaining documents in hard copy or they want to wait until they can be burned on to a disk, and I owe them the answer of when I can best estimate the technical process of burning those on to a disk will be completed. I expect to get that information after today's status conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So that would be hard copy in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, or within a reasonable time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And that would be all the disclosure material disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, well, that will be a start.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Judge May, another issue was raised at the conference that we had last month was the issue of video materials, and I had outlined to Your Honour that there were some film clips that we had disclosed to the Defence for which there were no translations, no transcripts. And as I outlined to Your Honour at the last conference, it was agreed by the parties that the Defence would prepare transcripts of those for which there were no transcripts, and they would forward those to us, and we would submit those to CLSS for translation. So I am waiting for receipt of those transcripts from those video clips for which there is no transcript. And upon receipt of those, I will submit those directly to CLSS for translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So the scheme is the Defence would provide B/C/S transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And you would have them translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct. The next item was the issue of reciprocal discovery, and at the last conference, I undertook to provide the Plavsic Defence with indexes of materials they had requested by the 15th of November, 2001. And we were delayed by one day. But with the consent of the Defence, I provided Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. those indexes to the Defence on the 16th of November, 2001. Lastly, I can report to Your Honours that on the 26th of November of this year, we produced a Rule 68 production to the Defence in which we identified materials that fell possibly within the ambit of that rule. And I do believe, Mr. President, that that concludes all of the items that we had discussed. In the interim time, I can report to Your Honours that there is an additional matter, and that is that many of our witnesses that we have identified in the course of these pre-trial proceedings have been witnesses who testified in other cases. And we have approximately 500 audiotapes of previous ICTY testimony, and I have suggested to the Defence a compromise position in that. I've given them an index. I've identified a portion of those witnesses for whom we have transcripts of their testimony. The Defence is in a position to review those transcripts, and if they want the audio portion of the testimony of the witness in B/C/S, then they will inform me that they want that audiotape, and we will copy it for them and produce it to them. So I'm waiting to hear from the Defence as to which of those previous testimonies in B/C/S they would like us to copy on to tape. The alternative is, of course, for us to copy 500 audiotapes per accused, a total of 1.000 audiotapes, and I believe that that would be essentially a waste of the Tribunal's resources. I don't think the Defence will listen to 500 audiotapes in total. I think they will listen to the audiotapes they want to hear. They will identify those to us. We will copy those audiotapes and make them available to the Defence. So that is something that wasn't raised at the last conference but raised in the interim time, and the -- we're working on the resolution of that particular issue as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are these witnesses whose evidence you're going to rely on or merely evidence which you think should be disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Evidence that we think should be disclosed and evidence that we may rely on. So it falls under both categories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Will you be seeking, do you think, in due course to put the transcripts in?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We may. Correct, Judge May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Two other matters. There was a motion -- I think there's a motion from Mr. Brashich of the 28th of November to which you have to respond within the next day or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I thought I had addressed all of the issues, but if Your Honour has a copy of the transcript and can refer me to the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a motion of the 28th of November for access to some supporting material.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Judge May, I have a copy of that before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And also, a further motion for production of statements made by a co-accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We will be responding to that in due course. As to the motion to receive statements of the co-accused -- Judge May, we will be filing written responses in due course as to each of the motions raised by Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The final matter is the clarification of the indictment. You said at the meeting that you would probably provide an amended indictment by the end of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But the matter was left over to the status conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We intend to file an amended indictment by the 31st of January. It is still our intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Are there any orders which you seek?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And perhaps I can put this to you: As things stand, is this case on course or is it not on course for a hearing in the autumn of next year? Is there any reason why it shouldn't be?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Realistically, we are making enormous steps toward a trial that could commence in the fall. What is unknown to us is what this new translation regime brings to us. We will be inquiring, as Mr. Tieger said, as to whether this means we will have fewer documents translated or more documents. At the same time, we will be working vigorously to try to reduce the number of documents that need to be translated, in addition to which we will be trying to narrow the focus of this indictment, which could also result in this case hitting the mark of trial in the fall. So I would say at this time, projecting ahead with those unknowns, particularly the language translation, I would say that we are on course. The Defence will have at least in untranslated form the majority of our documents. When I say the majority, they will have all of the exhibits we have identified now and the interim time. And if we continue to identify additional documents, we will turn those over to the Defence upon receipt and upon proper identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the date now for the pre-trial brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have not selected a date for the pre-trial brief. I would kindly request the Court to reserve fixing a date for the pre-trial brief until the next status conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I note that I said at the meeting that next March would be a suitable date for a pre-trial brief. We will have to fix a pre-trial conference obviously before then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Judge May, it seems to me that the -- a March pre-trial brief might be a little premature. When we amend the indictment on the 31st of January, there may be some motions, although it's our hope that there will be very few motions relating to the form of the indictment, if any. But it's the translation backlog that causes us the most concern in a sense that we don't quite have a firm handle on how far advanced we're going to be on that issue. And that's a fundamental issue that impacts on our ability to prepare properly a pre-trial brief and impacts on the Defence's ability to understand the case against them. They will have, of course, all of the documents at hand very soon, but they will be untranslated. My suggestion, if the Court please, would be to defer the fixing of a pre-trial brief. I think March is too early. I tried to sketch out in this realm of speculation when we would have all of the documents completed, a date for a filing of a pre-trial brief from the Prosecutor. My date is the 30th of June with the Defence pre-trial brief at the end of August. But those are dates that, again, I'm uncomfortable with, given the state of play with the translations. I think those dates -- I defer to my colleagues from the Defence. They are best able to comment on their views as to when our pre-trial brief should be filed and when theirs should be filed. But I think the problems that confront both sides are common. They relate to the translation backlog. And if we are to file something that is useful, intelligent, and helpful to the Court and to each side, then we have to have a firm grasp of the documents in a language that we, the lawyers, understand. That is my suggestion, Judge May, if we could defer scheduling that at this point in time. And if you could await -- if Your Honours could await hearing from the parties further on as we progress through these issues, I think that would be very helpful to both of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think that may well be a sensible course. But it must be understood that this trial must come on sooner rather than later. And next fall is the target date. If the translation problems are getting in the way of that, then they must be resolved. So if there are further difficulties, you can perhaps report them to the Court as soon as they emerge and we'll have to consider them together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We will do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'll hear from the Defence. Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. The Defence really has nothing further to add to Mr. Harmon's statements at this present time, and we of course reserve our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Pavich.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: Nor does the Plavsic Defence, Your Honour. We have an institutional problem and it requires institutional solutions, and I think we're all working toward that end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Court would obviously encourage cooperation between counsel towards resolving these problems. Now, it remains for me to fix a date for the next conference, but before I do that, is there anything that anybody wants to raise in relation to detention or matters of that sort? Mr. Brashich, do you or your client want to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: If I may have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Nothing at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We will fix the next Status Conference for the 8th of March. Meanwhile, there will be meetings with the Senior Legal Officer to ensure that progress continues. The Court will rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 3.03 p.m.
